 Darkness is setting in across the U.S. For a lot of sports businesses, that's not a bad thing. 
 Design by Grace Hughes, Photos by Patrick Smith/Getty Images), Sam Hodde/Getty Images 
 The U.S. adopting daylight saving time more than 100 years ago offered business opportunities for MLB, opening the door for games to be played later in the day before stadium lights were widespread. Now, President Donald Trump ’s current efforts to make DST permanent year-round could provide a similar lift to pro golf’s bottom line.
 On Sunday, Americans will once again set their clocks back an hour, trading evening sunlight for more morning rays, despite Trump’s support for the Sunshine Protection Act, which could make summer time permanent across the U.S. The bill passed in the House in July but has stalled in the Senate.
 “The United States Senate is letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it,” Trump said on Truth Social Monday. “Most people are demanding light in the evening, but ALL want not to change their clocks anymore.”
 Trump previously wrote the practice “costs our Country a fortune, is bad for Crime, stress on people, Sports, and just about everything else you can imagine.”
 Trump has been in favor of the move since at least 2019. And he now has an ally on the issue in the man atop the professional competitive golf business.
 “Permanent daylight saving time (DST) would expand access to golf at a time when the game is more popular than ever,” PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp wrote in a letter to the President earlier this month. The CEO of the National Golf Course Owners Association of America, meanwhile, has testified that permanent DST could boost the golf economy 5% “overnight.” More light could benefit golf’s after-school set, boosting a trend that has seen regular golf play increase 73% among 13-to-17-year-olds between 2019 and 2025, according to one recent study.
 Rolapp’s support for permanent daylight saving time is partially motivated by TV considerations, as golf is one of the biggest sports unable to offer content during primetime TV windows. “Usable afternoon daylight in the fall and winter would give our broadcast partners flexibility to extend live coverage of finishing holes, avoid awkward lighting situations in late rounds, and deliver a better overall product for the millions of fans who tune in each week,” the former NFL media boss wrote in his letter to POTUS. He is currently re-structuring the PGA Tour’s schedule to gain more eyeballs on weekends when football isn’t being played. Many other sports businesses, meanwhile, are set up to capitalize on a few cold, dark months.
 Daylight saving debates stretch back more than a century. In 1918, politicians shifted clocks with an eye toward war-time efficiency. Baseball’s entrepreneurs, however, saw the move as an opportunity to play games slightly later, giving fans a chance to attend after work while still playing nine innings before the sun went down. National League president John K. Tener spoke at multiple daylight-saving rallies as the option was considered, The New York Times reported. Few games ultimately ended up shifting, however, after clubs were reminded that the whole point of the effort was to increase labor output. One official called those moving ballgame schedules around “slackers of the worst type.”
 Daylight saving practices wouldn’t be permanently standardized until 1966. DST was later expanded from six to seven months in 1986. Warmer April games likely contributed to MLB’s 6% jump in per-game attendance year-over-year for that month in 1987.
 At the same time, the golf industry estimated an extra month of evening sun would mean as much as $400 million in added equipment sales and green fees.
 TV executives, on the other hand, came to dread springing forward. Up against extra hours of post-work light, TV viewership could drop as much as 10% in the days immediately following a time jump. However, usage often settled back into pre-change patterns. And these days, the effect has gotten weaker—after all, we’re on our screens day and night now. Audience analysts from Fox and ESPN said the impact of time changes on TV ratings are minimal, dwarfed by changes in how viewership is measured today.
 In the fall, programmers rarely see a dramatic rise in viewership aligned to the earlier sunsets, though some data does indicate that people spend less money—and therefore likely less time—out and about as winter sets in.
 “I would classify daylight saving in the same category as things like cold weather, inclement weather—things that tend to push people indoors,” Fox Sports EVP for strategy and consumer insights Ben Valenta said. “And we tend to look at it like there’s a slight uptick in (TV) usage, so I’d say it’s generally a tailwind, but I think it’s pretty small.”
 DST was extended another four weeks in 2005. Starting in November, several regions in Canada are ending their clock-changing ways and moving to permanent daylight saving time. People in those areas won’t have to worry about switching their body clocks twice a year, but they will be out of sync with neighbors south of the border. Numerous NHL games will now start at a slightly different hour as the league adjusts its schedule to account for the new policy. And yet, Canadians fan are still likely to make time for hockey, whatever time it is.
 Anthony Crupi contributed reporting.
